source_refs.note: Topic 8.4, printed pages 183-184: water potential, solute potential, pressure potential and their sum.

blocks.text: Water molecules possess kinetic energy: in liquid or gaseous form they move about rapidly and randomly from place to place. The greater the concentration of water molecules in a system, the greater is their total kinetic energy; this is the water potential, symbolised by the Greek letter psi (Ψw). In plant cells two factors determine the water potential: the solute potential (Ψs) and the pressure potential (Ψp).

Pure water has the maximum water potential, which by definition is zero. Water moves from a region of higher Ψw to a region of lower Ψw. All solutions have a lower Ψw than pure water and so have a negative Ψw (at atmospheric pressure and a defined temperature). Osmosis can therefore be defined as the movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.

blocks.title: Solute potential (Ψs)
blocks.text: The solute potential, or osmotic potential, is the change in the water potential of a system due to the presence of solute molecules. It is always negative: the more solute molecules present, the lower (more negative) the Ψs.

blocks.title: Pressure potential (Ψp)
blocks.text: The part of the water potential due to the pressure exerted by water. If a pressure greater than atmospheric is applied to pure water or a solution, its water potential increases. When water enters a plant cell by osmosis, pressure builds up inside, making the cell turgid and raising the pressure potential.

The total water potential is the sum of the solute potential and the pressure potential: Ψw = Ψs + Ψp. Using water potential, the tendency of water to move between any two systems can be measured, not just from cell to cell in a plant but also from soil to root, from leaf to air and from soil to air. The steeper the potential gradient, the faster water flows along it.

blocks.caption: Water potential and its parts
rows: Zero for pure water; negative for solutions
Total tendency of water to move out of a system
Lowering of Ψw by dissolved solutes
Raising of Ψw by pressure, as when a cell wall presses on its contents

blocks.prompt: Cell A has a solute potential of minus 800 kPa and a pressure potential of 300 kPa; cell B has a solute potential of minus 600 kPa and a pressure potential of 200 kPa. Which way does water move between them, and why?
blocks.explanation: Ψw of A is minus 800 plus 300, that is minus 500 kPa; Ψw of B is minus 600 plus 200, that is minus 400 kPa. Water moves from the higher water potential to the lower, so from B (minus 400) to A (minus 500).

items: Water potential (Ψw) is the tendency of water to move; pure water is zero, all solutions negative, and water flows from higher to lower Ψw. Osmosis is this flow through a partially permeable membrane.
Ψw = Ψs + Ψp: solute potential is always negative and falls with more solute; pressure potential rises as a turgid cell presses on its wall.
The gradient of Ψw drives water from soil to root, cell to cell, and leaf to air; the steeper the gradient, the faster the flow.
